fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jehoram, king of Judah, walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, just as the house of Ahab had done. Ahab was Israel's king (1 Kings 16:29), and Jehoram married one of his daughters. The text puts those two things side by side, and I'll let you do the math.

Close, friend, because Jehoshaphat was Jehoram's father and the king before him. But verse 18 says Jehoram walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, just as the house of Ahab had done. That's the road the text names.

Elisha is a prophet (1 Kings 19:16), but he isn't mentioned anywhere in these verses. What verse 18 says is that Jehoram walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, just as the house of Ahab had done. That's the road he picked. Looking for a prophet in this verse is like looking for a chocolate chip in a plain sugar cookie.
True, friend. Verse 18 says Jehoram "…did evil in the sight of the LORD." The text comes right out and says it. I think that's a heavy thing to read about a king.

You got it, baker. Verse 19 says He had promised to maintain a lamp for David and his descendants forever. David was Israel's king long before this (2 Samuel 5:3). So the reason is a promise, and the text names it plainly.
That's it, baker. Verse 20 says Edom rebelled against the hand of Judah and "…appointed their own king." They set up their own leader, like a crew that quits and opens its own shop across the street.

Right on target, baker. When the Edomites surrounded Jehoram and his chariot commanders at Zair, he "…rose up and attacked by night." The text gives the action and leaves out the plan, so I'll leave it out too.
No messenger here, baker. Verse 21 says he rose up and attacked by night. The text shows him attacking, and it doesn't mention any message.

I wish it were true for him, friend, but verse 21 says otherwise. It says, "His troops, however, fled to their homes." That word "however" tells you the turn. The text says Jehoram attacked, and says his troops fled to their homes.

Yes, baker. Verse 22 says "…to this day Edom has been in rebellion against the hand of Judah." The writer is telling you it was still going when this was written. Libnah rebelled at the same time too.

That's not what verse 22 says, friend. It says "…to this day Edom has been in rebellion against the hand of Judah." So as of the writer's day, Edom was still in rebellion. I think that's one stubborn dough.
No payments are mentioned, baker. The text says "…to this day Edom has been in rebellion against the hand of Judah." The writer says the rebellion was still going when this was written.

Jezreel does show up later in this passage, baker, but not here. It's where King Joram goes to recover from his wounds (2 Kings 8:29). Jehoram, king of Judah, was buried in the City of David (2 Kings 8:24). Easy to mix up two kings with almost the same name.

Ben-hadad was a king of Aram (2 Kings 8:7), but he isn't connected to Athaliah in this passage. Verse 26 says she was the granddaughter of Omri king of Israel. I'd say you grabbed a different king from the cookie jar.
Jehu isn't named in this passage, friend. Verse 28 says Ahaziah went with Joram son of Ahab. That's the traveling partner the text gives.

Elisha, a prophet (1 Kings 19:16), isn't named in these verses, baker. Verse 28 says Ahaziah went with Joram son of Ahab to fight against Hazael king of Aram. That's the pair the text names heading to Ramoth-gilead.
Yes, baker. Verse 28 says "…the Arameans wounded Joram." Joram is king of Israel and the son of Ahab. In the next verse he returns to Jezreel to recover.
That's right, baker. Verse 29 says Ahaziah went down to Jezreel "…to visit Joram son of Ahab, because Joram had been wounded." Think of dropping by with a plate of cookies when somebody's laid up.

No anointing in this verse, baker. Verse 29 says Ahaziah went down to Jezreel to visit Joram, because Joram had been wounded. The text gives a visit as the reason for the trip, and anointing isn't mentioned.
